Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest,
O stranger worn with toil,
To a land of all lands the goodliest
Colonus’ glistening soil.
’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale,
Who hid in her bower, among
The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale,
Trilleth her ceaseless song;
And she loves, where the clustering berries nod
O’er a sunless, windless glade,
The spot by no mortal footstep trod,
The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god,
Where he holds each night his revels wild
With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.

anchorPassages.text:
Yet another gift, of all gifts the most
Prized by our fatherland, we boast—
The might of the horse, the might of the sea;
Our fame, Poseidon, we owe to thee,
Son of Kronos, our king divine,
Who in these highways first didst fit
For the mouth of horses the iron bit;
Thou too hast taught us to fashion meet
For the arm of the rower the oar-blade fleet,
Swift as the Nereids’ hundred feet
As they dance along the brine.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening…” slowly and put it in my own words: The elders greet the worn stranger by praising the land itself: a country famous for horses, the goodliest of lands, Colonus with glistening soil. Next, craft. I notice the ode speaks to him (“Thou hast come… O stranger worn with toil”) and then lifts the eye to the ground under his feet. The strongest word is “glistening”: “glistening” makes the soil shine, a visual welcome after the fear and argument of the earlier scenes. Then, effect. What do lines 695–698 reveal about the Colonus ode? My answer: The Colonus ode reveals a land of light on the ground: this praise of Colonus is a song about a place that can receive a worn stranger, not a song about battle.

items.text: What does the Olive Planter do, in the ode's account of the tree?
items.lookFor: He tends the plant
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He tends the plant.

items.text: What did Poseidon first fit, in these highways, for the mouths of horses?
items.lookFor: The iron bit
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The iron bit.

items.text: What has he taught this people to fashion for the rower's arm?
items.lookFor: The oar-blade fleet
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The oar-blade fleet.

items.text: Why place a hymn of praise right after Theseus' welcome?
items.lookFor: It celebrates the land that has just taken the stranger in: the ode turns Theseus’s private pledge into the community’s public praise, addressed to the guest.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Theseus has just promised protection, and the elders who once cried “Begone!” now speak to Oedipus directly: “Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil” (lines 695–696). Placing the hymn here shows the community accepting what its king decided, and tells the stranger what kind of place has received him.

items.text: What does “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” suggest about the Colonus ode? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: The undying olive stands for a city that renews itself and cannot be cut down by age or by its enemies, so it can shelter a guest.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The olive is the ode’s image of endurance: “Nor youth nor withering age destroys / The plant that the Olive Planter tends” (lines 726–727). The ode suggests that Athens, like its olive, renews itself and cannot be cut down by age or enemies, which is why it can safely shelter an old man whom Thebes wants back.

items.text: Find one example of imagery in “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”. What does it reveal about the Colonus ode that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: One image (the nightingale in the ivy, the sleepless fountains, the olive, Poseidon’s bit and oar) and what it shows beyond a plain statement: a land that keeps renewing itself.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: “And never the sleepless fountains cease / That feed Cephisus’ stream” (lines 713–714). The never-failing springs make the land itself seem alive and generous, always giving. A plain statement that Colonus is fertile would not carry that sense of a place that keeps renewing itself, which is exactly what a worn-out stranger lacks.

items.text: How does the setting in “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” shape what we understand about the Colonus ode?
items.lookFor: How the ode’s setting, a plain favoured by the Muses and the goddess of love and kept by gods, presents Colonus as divinely loved, so that rest here means divine favour, not just shelter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode says “the Muses’ quire will never disdain / To visit this heaven-favoured plain” (lines 717–718). The setting is not just pleasant; it is visited and loved by gods. That shapes the welcome: a stranger resting here rests under divine favour, which answers the elders’ earlier fear that his presence would offend the powers of the place.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Thou hast come to…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from the opening lines with their connotations, such as “steed-famed” (a heroic reputation), “worn” (exhaustion), “goodliest” or “glistening,” showing a welcome that pairs the land’s glory with the stranger’s need.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The word “steed-famed” (line 695) gives the land a heroic reputation, while “worn” (line 696) names the stranger’s exhaustion. The pairing makes the land’s fame and the stranger’s need fit together: a famous place offers rest to a tired man.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The ode’s turn from natural beauty (song, water, flowers) to civic strength (the olive feared by enemies, Poseidon’s horse and oar), and its effect: the welcome becomes a promise that this land can defend its guest.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn comes at “And here there grows, unpruned, untamed, / Terror to foemen’s spear” (lines 720–721). Until then the ode praises song, water and flowers; from here it praises strength, ending with “The might of the horse, the might of the sea” (line 731). The effect is to remind the audience, just after a threat from Thebes has been announced, that this land can fight for its guest.

items.text: How does “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” build on “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal link: Oedipus’s warning in Episode 1 that all strength decays is answered by an olive that age cannot destroy, sung now because Theseus has pledged protection.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In Episode 1 Oedipus warned that “Earth’s might decays, the might of men decays” (line 632). The ode answers with an olive that “Nor youth nor withering age destroys” (line 726). Because Theseus has just pledged protection, the elders now sing of a place whose strength does not decay. The fear in Episode 1 produces this hopeful reply.

items.text: In “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the Colonus ode, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive inferred from the elders’ praise: they claim to welcome the stranger, but most of the ode praises their own land, suggesting civic pride and a wish to make up for their first hostility.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders claim simply to welcome the stranger (“Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest,” line 695), but the ode spends far more lines on Colonus than on him, ending with “Our fame, Poseidon, we owe to thee” (line 732). A fair inference is that civic pride, and a wish to repair their first hostility, drive the song: by praising the land, they show the stranger what his hosts are worth.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (What would you name if you wrote a song praising your own home?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer that compares the student’s list with what the elders actually choose (birds, river, sacred flowers, the olive, horses and ships), noting that the ode praises strength as well as beauty.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: My first list was things I like about home: food, friends, a park. The ode made me add what protects a home. The elders praise “the clear-voiced nightingale” (line 699) but also the olive that is “Terror to foemen’s spear” (line 721) and the oar their people learned to make (lines 736–737). A home worth praising both comforts and defends.

items.text: Where does tone / mood appear in “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”, and how does it connect the Colonus ode to the larger concern with law against force?
items.lookFor: Where the mood shifts from serene to proud and martial, and how that connects to law against force: the strength the ode praises is controlled strength (the bit that tames horses), not raiding.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The mood is peaceful through the glade and fountains, then turns proud and martial with the olive that is “Terror to foemen’s spear” (line 721). Even the strength the ode praises is ordered strength: Poseidon “first didst fit / For the mouth of horses the iron bit” (lines 734–735), taming force rather than letting it loose. That connects to law against force: Athens is pictured as a power that controls its own strength.

items.text: Is the ode about Oedipus, Athens, or both? Defend your reading.
items.lookFor: A defended reading: mainly the land, but framed as an address to the stranger, with everything praised answering his need (rest, endurance, protection), plus a counter-reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: both, but Athens is the subject and Oedipus is the audience. Only the opening speaks to him (“O stranger worn with toil,” line 696); the rest praises the land. Yet everything praised answers his need: rest after toil, an olive that age cannot destroy for an old man, and a power that can protect a guest. Counter-line: a reader could argue that it is purely civic pride, since Oedipus is never named and the closing lines belong to Poseidon (lines 729–739).

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The undying olive stands for a city that endures. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand on the reading with two lines from the olive stanza (lines 720–728), perhaps qualifying that the olive is also a weapon and a gift defended by a goddess.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, and extend it. The olive is “Self-nurtured year by year” (line 724), so it does stand for endurance. But it is also “Terror to foemen’s spear” (line 721), and “the Grey-eyed Goddess herself defends” it (line 728). The city endures because its people and its goddess defend it, not only because it is old.

items.text: No character acts in “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”; the elders sing. Which gift or image the ode praises seems wisest to value most, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two things the ode praises, for example what best serves a stranger who needs rest and safety: the olive against the night revels. Give lines.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of what best serves a worn stranger, the olive is the wisest thing to value, since it “feeds our boys” (line 725) and age cannot destroy it. The least, by that standard, is the night revel of “the Bacchic god” (line 706), which delights but protects no one. A student using beauty as the standard could rank the nightingale’s “ceaseless song” (line 702) first instead.

items.text: You are directing “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the Colonus ode.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the chorus turning from Oedipus to the audience or a change of rhythm at the olive or the oar, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) On the opening lines (lines 695–696), have the elders face Oedipus, then slowly turn outward to the audience, so the welcome becomes the city praising itself. (2) At “The might of the horse, the might of the sea” (line 731), shift the music to a stronger beat and let the dancers mime rowing through the last lines. The audience feels the land’s power right after its gentleness.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 695–739: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Which river do the sleepless fountains feed? (The Cephisus, line 714.) Why/how: Why does the ode end with Poseidon’s gifts of horse and oar rather than with the grove? (It moves from beauty to the city’s strength.) Should/what if: If you were Oedipus, should this ode reassure you? (Answers weigh the strength promised here against the elders’ earlier fear.)

items.text: Connect “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”, with its focus on the Colonus ode, to death and blessing: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about death and blessing, the question’s theme. The ode itself is full of life, not death, so the link is weak here; a strong answer notes that Oedipus has already tied his blessing to his death and says what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is weak inside the ode, and the contrast matters. The ode is full of life: fountains that “swell earth’s bosom with quick increase” (line 715). But Oedipus has already said his benefit comes “When I am dead and thou hast buried me” (line 603). Sophocles would need to show how that promised blessing after death joins this land of living blessings.

items.text: Is the imagery in “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” effective in presenting the Colonus ode, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment of the imagery against a stated criterion (does it do dramatic work or only decorate?), with a line that meets the criterion and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because the images are chosen for this stranger. Rest, shade and endless water, “O’er a sunless, windless glade” (line 704), offer a weary wanderer what he lacks. Counter-line: the ode’s many gods and myths, such as “the Cyprian queen of the golden rein” (line 719) or the Nereids’ “hundred feet” (line 738), may read like a catalogue. That could feel heavy-handed unless the class sees it as a hometown hymn by a poet born at Colonus.

items.text: Compare how “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” treats the Colonus ode with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (a song, poem or speech praising a home or nation) and one thing the ode sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare “America the Beautiful,” which praises a land’s beauty and plenty. The ode sees something the anthem leaves implicit: praise of home is offered to a stranger, as a promise of what the home will give him (“Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest,” line 695). It ties a land’s worth to how it treats someone who is not its own.

items.text: Predict what “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, the olive feared by enemies and the earlier report that Creon is coming, about a coming test of the land’s strength, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: the ode stresses defence, with the olive as “Terror to foemen’s spear” (line 721). Clue 2: Ismene reported that “Creon comes to thee—and comes anon” (line 397). A reasonable prediction is that Creon will come and the land the elders just praised will have to show whether it can protect its guest. After reading, students judge whether the praise held up.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the Colonus ode?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a community praises its home to a newcomer it has just accepted, moving from comfort to strength. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: At a coastal town’s welcome evening, a choir sings to a newly settled exile about its lighthouse, orchards and fishing fleet. Two things must stay: the direct address to the newcomer (“O stranger worn with toil,” line 696), and the turn from gentle beauty to the town’s strength (lines 720–721), so the praise is also a promise of protection.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.
